```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# The ragg device writes smaller figure files; without it the default is used.
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
options(bayesEfron.use_cli = FALSE, width = 90)
```

In this vignette we compare bayesEfron with the empirical Bayes methods
in the ebnm package [@willwerscheid2025]. We apply both to the same data:
the 97 callback gaps of `vignette("bayesEfron")`, the 1,500 simulated
sites of `vignette("twin-towers")`, and further simulated data sets, from
which we estimate coverage.

Empirical Bayes is the most common way to shrink estimates that come
with standard errors [@robbins1956]. It works in two steps. First it
estimates the distribution of the true effects, $g$, from all the
estimates. Then it treats that estimate, $\hat g$, as if it were the
truth, and computes the posterior distribution of each effect under it.
An estimate used in this way is called a plug-in estimate. bayesEfron
starts from the same sampling model and the same idea, but differs in
the second step. It gives $g$ a prior distribution, obtains a posterior
distribution for it, and averages the posterior distribution of each
effect over that uncertainty [@lee2025]. We want to see how much this
changes the results, and what else differs between the methods.

## Setup

We ran the comparison in advance, with the script
`data-raw/ebnm-comparison.R` in the source repository, and stored its
results in the package, so you don't need ebnm to follow this vignette.
After loading bayesEfron we read the stored results and take out the
four tables of results.

```{r stored}
library(bayesEfron)

stored <- readRDS(system.file("examples", "ebnm_comparison.rds",
                              package = "bayesEfron"))
krw <- stored$krw$table            # callback gaps
twin <- stored$twin$table          # simulated sites
panels <- stored$panels$table      # simulated data sets, unequal standard errors
equal <- stored$equal_se$repeated  # simulated data sets, equal standard errors
```

Two small functions format the numbers in the tables: `num()` sets the
number of decimals, and `with_se()` puts a standard error in parentheses
after its value.

```{r helpers}
num <- function(x, digits = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
with_se <- function(x, se, digits = 3) {
  sprintf("%s (%s)", num(x, digits), num(se, digits))
}
```

```{r lookup, include = FALSE}
# Row names and a lookup function for the numbers in the text.
rownames(krw) <- krw$method
rownames(twin) <- twin$method
panel <- function(K, method) panels[panels$K == K & panels$method == method, ]
```

## A plug-in version of a bayesEfron fit

For a bayesEfron fit we can separate the two steps by using the
posterior mean of $g$ as a plug-in estimate. `as_normalmix()` returns
that posterior mean in the form that ebnm uses for a prior distribution.
We apply it to `krw_fit`, the fit of the 97 callback gaps from
`vignette("bayesEfron")`.

```{r as-normalmix}
g_hat <- as_normalmix(krw_fit)
class(g_hat)
str(unclass(g_hat)[c("pi", "mean", "sd")], give.attr = FALSE)
```

As the output shows, the result is a mixture of point masses at the
`r length(g_hat$pi)` grid points (`mean`), with their probabilities in
`pi`. If we pass it to ebnm with `fix_g = TRUE`, ebnm computes the
posterior distributions of the effects as if this one $g$ were the
truth. The call needs ebnm and is not run here.

```{r plug-in, eval = FALSE}
plugged <- ebnm::ebnm_npmle(krw_discrimination$yi, krw_discrimination$sei,
                            g_init = g_hat, fix_g = TRUE)
```

In the tables below, the rows labeled "g of bayesEfron, plugged in" are
fits of this kind. They use the same $g$ as the rows labeled
"bayesEfron" but leave out its uncertainty. Their means and standard
deviations come from ebnm, and their intervals are computed from that
$g$ in the way that bayesEfron computes its own, so the two rows differ
only by the uncertainty about $g$.

## Methods and settings

All the methods are listed with their calls in `stored$settings`. In the
calls, `x` and `s` are the estimates and their standard errors.

```{r methods}
knitr::kable(stored$settings, col.names = c("Method", "Call"))
```

The first six rows are ebnm prior families: no shrinkage, a normal
distribution, a scale mixture of normals, the adaptive shrinkage (ash)
prior from the ashr package, a unimodal distribution, and the
nonparametric maximum likelihood estimate (NPMLE) [@kiefer1956]. We
explain the other rows where they are used.

Three choices make the fits comparable.

- We estimate the location of each prior family (`mode = "estimate"`),
  because by default ebnm centers the prior at zero.
- Every interval is an equal-tailed 90% interval. For ebnm we take the
  5% and 95% sample quantiles of 4,000 draws from each posterior
  distribution, because its `confint()` method returns a highest density
  interval.
- We give the ash prior normal components and fit it without the penalty
  that ashr puts on its weights by default.

Efron's estimator, in the last row, appears only in the last table of
results. The ebnm function for it, `ebnm_deconvolver()`, calls the
deconvolveR package [@narasimhan2020] and takes z-scores and no standard
errors. When the standard errors differ, a fit to the z-scores estimates
the distribution of the effects divided by their standard errors, which
is a different quantity. So we compare this estimator on data whose
standard errors are all equal.

An empirical Bayes fit of these data takes a fraction of a second. By
comparison, the bayesEfron fits took
`r num(krw["bayesEfron", "seconds"], 1)` seconds for the 97 firms and
`r num(twin["bayesEfron", "seconds"], 0)` seconds for the 1,500
simulated sites, including the pilot fit that sets the range of the
grid. We do not show these times again in the tables below.

## Callback gaps at 97 firms

We do not know the true gaps, so we compare each method with the
bayesEfron fit, `krw_fit`. Below we round the columns of `krw` that make
this comparison and print them.

```{r krw}
shown <- data.frame(
  method = krw$method, correlation = krw$correlation,
  largest_difference = krw$largest_difference_in_se, sd_ratio = krw$sd_ratio,
  length_ratio = krw$length_ratio, log_likelihood = krw$loglik
)
shown[2:5] <- round(shown[2:5], 3)
shown$log_likelihood <- round(shown$log_likelihood, 1)
knitr::kable(shown, col.names = c("Method", "Correlation of posterior means",
                                  "Largest difference (standard errors)",
                                  "Ratio of posterior SD", "Ratio of interval length",
                                  "Log likelihood"))
```

```{r krw-facts, include = FALSE}
sites <- site_summary(krw_fit)
ebnm_rows <- krw[1:6, ]
plugged <- krw["g of bayesEfron, plugged in", ]
stopifnot(
  abs(krw["bayesEfron", "mean_sd"] - mean(sites$sd)) < 1e-12,
  abs(krw["bayesEfron", "mean_length"] - mean(sites$upper - sites$lower)) < 1e-12,
  all(ebnm_rows$correlation > 0.95), which.max(krw$loglik) == 6L,
  all(ebnm_rows$sd_ratio[-1] < 1), plugged$sd_ratio > 0.99, plugged$length_ratio > 0.99,
  plugged$length_ratio < 1,
  diff(range(krw$loglik[!krw$method %in% c("NPMLE", "No shrinkage", "bayesEfron")])) < 1,
  max(krw[c(1:6, 7), "seconds"]) < 1, max(twin$seconds[1:8]) < 1
)
```

For each method the table has:

- the correlation of its posterior means with the bayesEfron posterior
  means;
- the largest difference between the two, in units of the firm's
  standard error;
- its mean posterior standard deviation, as a ratio to the bayesEfron
  value;
- the mean length of its 90% intervals, also as a ratio to the bayesEfron
  value;
- the marginal log likelihood of the 97 estimates under its estimate of
  $g$.

A ratio below 1 means smaller than bayesEfron.

Across methods the posterior means agree closely. Every correlation is
above 0.95, and among the six ebnm prior families the NPMLE is the
closest, at
`r num(krw["NPMLE", "correlation"])`. The intervals differ more. The
NPMLE intervals are
`r num(100 * (1 - krw["NPMLE", "length_ratio"]), 0)`% shorter than the
bayesEfron intervals, and the normal fit's intervals are
`r num(100 * (1 - krw["Normal", "length_ratio"]), 0)`% shorter.

This difference does not come from the uncertainty about $g$, as the
plug-in row shows. Leaving that uncertainty out makes the bayesEfron
intervals only `r num(100 * (1 - plugged$length_ratio), 1)`% shorter.
For these data, the shape of the estimated $g$ matters far more for the
intervals than the uncertainty about it.

The NPMLE has the largest log likelihood, as it must among distributions
on its grid. All the others, including the $g$ of bayesEfron in the
plug-in row, are within one unit of each other.

To compare the estimates of $g$ themselves we plot them as distribution
functions, which can be compared between a smooth estimate and a
discrete one. We take the distribution functions of three ebnm estimates
from `stored$krw$cdf` and pass them to `plot_g()` in its `compare`
argument, with the gaps in percentage points (`scale = 100`).

```{r krw-cdf, fig.alt = "The distribution function of the estimated distribution of callback gaps with its band, and those of the nonparametric, normal and unimodal empirical Bayes fits."}
curves <- stored$krw$cdf
others <- lapply(c(NPMLE = "NPMLE", Normal = "Normal", Unimodal = "Unimodal"),
                 function(method) curves[curves$method == method, c("x", "cdf")])
plot_g(krw_fit, type = "cdf", compare = others, scale = 100)
```

```{r krw-cdf-facts, include = FALSE}
# How far the distribution functions of the empirical Bayes fits leave the
# band of the fit.
band <- curves[curves$method == "bayesEfron", ]
outside <- vapply(c("Normal", "NPMLE", "Unimodal"), function(method) {
  curve <- curves[curves$method == method, ]
  stopifnot(identical(curve$x, band$x))
  max(pmax(band$lower - curve$cdf, curve$cdf - band$upper, 0))
}, numeric(1))
print(outside)
stopifnot(outside[["Normal"]] < 0.0002, outside[["NPMLE"]] > 0.1, outside[["Unimodal"]] > 0.1)
firms <- stored$krw$firms
in_every_list <- names(which(table(firms$firm) == length(unique(firms$method))))
print(length(unique(firms$firm))); print(in_every_list)
```

Only the bayesEfron estimate has a band. The NPMLE is a step function
with a few jumps, which is the form that an NPMLE takes, and the
unimodal estimate has a large jump at its mode. Between their jumps
these two curves leave the band, by up to `r num(outside[["NPMLE"]], 2)`
and `r num(outside[["Unimodal"]], 2)` in probability, as a discrete
estimate must when it is compared with a smooth one. By contrast, the
normal curve stays within the band, to within 0.0002 in probability. On
this evidence, the data do not exclude a normal distribution of the gaps.

The methods also largely agree on which firms are at the top. If we list
the 10 firms with the largest posterior means for each of the 8 rows
(`stored$krw$firms`), we get `r length(unique(firms$firm))` firms in
all, and `r length(in_every_list)` of them are in every list.

## Simulated sites with known effects

The true effects of the 1,500 simulated sites are known and lie in two
groups, so here we can judge each fit against the truth. We print four
measures from `twin`.

```{r twin}
shown <- data.frame(
  method = twin$method, rmse = round(twin$rmse, 3),
  inside = with_se(twin$inclusion, twin$inclusion_se),
  length = round(twin$mean_length, 2), w1 = round(twin$w1, 3)
)
knitr::kable(shown, col.names = c("Method", "RMSE of posterior means",
                                  "Proportion inside 90% interval (SE)", "Mean length",
                                  "Distance of the estimate of g"),
             align = "lrrrr")
```

```{r twin-facts, include = FALSE}
truth <- twin_towers$theta_true
sites <- site_summary(twin_towers_fit)
own <- twin["bayesEfron", ]
stopifnot(
  abs(own$rmse - sqrt(mean((sites$mean - truth)^2))) < 1e-12,
  abs(own$inclusion - mean(truth >= sites$lower & truth <= sites$upper)) < 1e-12,
  abs(own$rmse - twin["NPMLE", "rmse"]) < 0.001,
  twin["NPMLE", "inclusion"] < 0.8,
  abs(twin["Known g", "inclusion"] - 0.9) < 2 * twin["Known g", "inclusion_se"],
  abs(own$inclusion - 0.9) < 2 * own$inclusion_se,
  own$w1 == min(twin$w1[!twin$method %in% c("Known g", "No shrinkage",
                                            "bayesEfron, range from the true effects")]),
  twin["Normal", "rmse"] > own$rmse + 0.03
)
```

The first measure is the root mean squared error (RMSE) of the posterior
means. The second is the proportion of the true effects inside the 90%
intervals, with its standard error (`inclusion` and `inclusion_se` in the
stored tables). The third is the mean length of those intervals, and the
fourth is the Wasserstein distance between the estimate of $g$ and the
true effects, which is the area between their two distribution functions
in the units of the effects. The row "Known g" uses the true
distribution itself and shows what is attainable, and the last row takes
the range of its grid from the true effects.

The methods fall into groups. The normal fit, the scale mixture and the
ash fit have an RMSE near `r num(twin["Normal", "rmse"], 2)`, because
they shrink toward one center and the effects have two. The unimodal fit
does somewhat better, at `r num(twin["Unimodal", "rmse"], 2)`. Both the
NPMLE and bayesEfron reach `r num(own$rmse)`, close to the
`r num(twin["Known g", "rmse"])` of the true distribution. They differ
in their intervals, however: the NPMLE intervals contain
`r num(100 * twin["NPMLE", "inclusion"], 0)`% of the true effects and
the bayesEfron intervals `r num(100 * own$inclusion, 0)`%.

Ignoring the uncertainty about $g$ does not explain why the NPMLE
intervals are too short. The true distribution itself, taken as known,
gives intervals that contain
`r num(100 * twin["Known g", "inclusion"], 0)`% of the true effects, and
the plug-in $g$ of bayesEfron gives
`r num(100 * twin["g of bayesEfron, plugged in", "inclusion"], 0)`%. We
think the reason is the form of the estimate. The NPMLE of $g$ is a
handful of point masses, and the posterior distribution of a site under
it is concentrated on those points. By contrast, the bayesEfron estimate
is smooth, and among the estimates that use only the data it is the
closest to the true effects.

## Coverage over simulated data sets

From one data set we learn little about coverage, which is the
proportion of true effects inside the intervals averaged over many data
sets. So we repeated the comparison on independent simulated data sets
from the same design, each with its own true effects: 20 with 1,500
sites and 100 with 100 sites. In the next table we print the means over
these data sets, from `panels`, with their Monte Carlo standard errors.

```{r panels}
shown <- data.frame(
  sites = panels$K, method = panels$method,
  rmse = with_se(panels$rmse, panels$rmse_se),
  inside = with_se(panels$inclusion, panels$inclusion_se),
  length = with_se(panels$mean_length, panels$mean_length_se)
)
knitr::kable(shown, col.names = c("Sites", "Method", "RMSE (SE)",
                                  "Coverage of 90% intervals (SE)", "Mean length (SE)"),
             align = "rlrrr")
```

```{r panels-facts, include = FALSE}
by_panel <- stored$panels$by_panel
paired <- function(K, second, measure) {
  a <- by_panel[by_panel$K == K & by_panel$method == "bayesEfron", ]
  b <- by_panel[by_panel$K == K & by_panel$method == second, ]
  stopifnot(identical(a$panel, b$panel))
  d <- a[[measure]] - b[[measure]]
  c(mean = mean(d), se = sd(d) / sqrt(length(d)))
}
extra_length <- function(K) {
  100 * paired(K, "g of bayesEfron, plugged in", "mean_length")[["mean"]] /
    panel(K, "g of bayesEfron, plugged in")$mean_length
}
rmse_gap <- function(K) paired(K, "NPMLE", "rmse")
stopifnot(
  all(abs(panels$inclusion[panels$method == "bayesEfron"] - 0.9) < 0.01),
  all(panels$inclusion[panels$method == "NPMLE"] < 0.8),
  extra_length(100) < 1, extra_length(1500) < 0.2,
  rmse_gap(100)[["mean"]] > 2 * rmse_gap(100)[["se"]],
  rmse_gap(1500)[["mean"]] > 2 * rmse_gap(1500)[["se"]],
  all(abs(panels$inclusion[panels$method == "Normal"] - 0.9) < 0.01)
)
print(c(extra_length(100), extra_length(1500)))
print(rbind(rmse_gap(100), rmse_gap(1500)))
```

At both sizes the bayesEfron intervals have coverage close to 0.90:
`r num(panel(100, "bayesEfron")$inclusion)` with 100 sites and
`r num(panel(1500, "bayesEfron")$inclusion)` with 1,500. For the NPMLE
the coverage is `r num(panel(100, "NPMLE")$inclusion, 2)` and
`r num(panel(1500, "NPMLE")$inclusion, 2)`.

Again the uncertainty about $g$ adds little to the site intervals. The
bayesEfron intervals are `r num(extra_length(100), 1)`% longer than the
plug-in intervals with 100 sites and
`r num(extra_length(1500), 2)`% longer with 1,500. We might have expected
more with only 100 sites, which leave $g$ quite uncertain. But most of
the posterior uncertainty about a single effect comes from its own
standard error, and the part that comes from $g$ is small in comparison.
For your own fit, `site_summary()` returns the two parts for every site
in the columns `sd_given_g` and `sd_about_g`.

In accuracy the NPMLE is slightly ahead. Its posterior means have an
RMSE that is lower than the bayesEfron RMSE by
`r num(100 * rmse_gap(100)[["mean"]] / panel(100, "bayesEfron")$rmse, 1)`%
with 100 sites and by
`r num(100 * rmse_gap(1500)[["mean"]] / panel(1500, "bayesEfron")$rmse, 1)`%
with 1,500. The normal fit has a single center, which does not suit
these effects, but its intervals still have coverage close to 0.90. It
pays in accuracy and in length: with 1,500 sites its intervals are
`r num(100 * (panel(1500, "Normal")$mean_length / panel(1500, "bayesEfron")$mean_length - 1), 0)`%
longer than the bayesEfron intervals.

## Equal standard errors and Efron's estimator

bayesEfron is the Bayesian form of the estimator of @efron2016, and the
two can be compared directly when the standard errors are equal. We
first added an error with standard deviation 1 to each true effect of
the 20 data sets with 1,500 sites. We then fitted the model and ran
`deconvolveR::deconv()` on the grid of that fit, with the same number of
spline functions and with the likelihood of the estimates themselves,
not of their counts in intervals. Finally we computed the posterior
distributions of the sites under the `deconv()` estimate of $g$. We
added these 20 data sets after we had seen the result for one such data
set. Their means are in `equal`, which we print next.

```{r equal}
shown <- data.frame(
  functions = equal$M, method = equal$method,
  rmse = with_se(equal$rmse, equal$rmse_se),
  inside = with_se(equal$inclusion, equal$inclusion_se),
  length = with_se(equal$mean_length, equal$mean_length_se, 2)
)
knitr::kable(shown, col.names = c("Spline functions", "Method", "RMSE (SE)",
                                  "Coverage of 90% intervals (SE)", "Mean length (SE)"),
             align = "rlrrr")
```

```{r equal-facts, include = FALSE}
own <- equal[equal$method == "bayesEfron", ]
efron <- equal[equal$method == "Efron's estimator", ]
one <- stored$equal_se$g
stopifnot(all(own$inclusion < 0.9 - 2 * own$inclusion_se),
          all(abs(efron$inclusion - 0.9) < 0.015),
          all(own$rmse < efron$rmse), all(own$mean_length < efron$mean_length),
          all(equal$rhat_max < 1.01), max(one$bayesEfron) > 1.1 * max(one$efron))
```

As before, the point estimates are nearly the same. Here the bayesEfron
intervals are the shorter ones, and their coverage falls short of 90%:
`r num(100 * own$inclusion[1], 1)`% with 6 spline functions and
`r num(100 * own$inclusion[2], 1)`% with 8, against
`r num(100 * efron$inclusion[1], 1)`% and
`r num(100 * efron$inclusion[2], 1)`% for Efron's estimator. All of
these fits converged, so this is a property of the estimates and not of
the sampler.

We have an explanation, but we have not tested it on its own. With
every standard error equal to 1, no site is precise enough to show the
shape of $g$ within a group. In the one such data set for which we kept
both estimates of $g$ (`stored$equal_se$g`), the posterior mean of $g$
is more peaked than the estimate that `deconv()` regularizes with its
penalty, and a more peaked $g$ gives narrower posterior distributions
for the sites.

We saw the lower coverage for one distribution of true effects, flat
within two groups, and for one size of error, so we do not know how far
it extends. The data sets with unequal standard errors from the same
distribution show no shortfall. Even so, you should not rely on the 90%
site intervals to have 90% coverage in every configuration, and data in
which no site is estimated precisely call for caution.

## Summary

If the posterior means of the sites are all you need, it matters little
whether you use a flexible empirical Bayes fit or bayesEfron, and an
empirical Bayes fit takes a fraction of a second. These results give no
reason to prefer the slower method for that purpose.

The methods differ in their estimates of the distribution of effects and
in the uncertainty that they attach to each effect. A normal prior is
adequate when the effects are roughly normal and misses the shape when
they are not. An NPMLE follows the shape with a few point masses, which
do well for means and poorly for intervals. bayesEfron gives a smooth
estimate of $g$, with a band that shows how much of its shape the data
determine, and site intervals that had coverage close to 0.90 in the
simulated data sets with unequal standard errors.

What set bayesEfron apart in these comparisons was the smoothness of its
estimate of $g$. Its intervals also average over the uncertainty about
$g$, which is part of the model, but the averaging changed them by less
than 1%.
